vignette:
At 27, Minh had been building a reputation as a sharp local journalist, the kind of reporter who could stay calm in chaotic rooms and notice what other people missed. That steadiness changed over the final year of a relationship that became physically abusive. The assaults often happened after arguments in cramped apartments and on evenings that ended with bus rides home, when his partner would turn cold and watchful in public, then violent once they were alone. Minh remembers one night especially clearly: the fluorescent light of the bus, the hiss of the doors, the press of male bodies standing in the aisle, and later the force of being hit hard enough that his ribs and shoulder throbbed. Those details have remained painfully alive for him, so that ordinary trauma-related reminders, riding the bus, or finding himself alone with a man can feel tied to the original danger rather than separate from it.

In the months after the relationship ended, these reminders did not stay as reminders. If a bus jerked to a stop or a man sat too close when he was riding across town for an interview, the memory arrived as if it were happening again in the present. After episodes like that, Minh began organizing his days around not being caught off guard again: he avoided buses when he could, left situations with men as soon as he felt the shift in his body, and once he got home he would replay what he believed he had done wrong, clamp down on any anger, and sometimes skip meals to force himself back into a sense of control. He did not describe it as “thinking about” what happened; he said it dropped him back into it. His chest and side would start to hurt in the same places he had been struck, and the rush of feeling was so intense that he would sometimes have to get off early or abandon what he was doing because he could not bear to stay with it. Because these episodes were so vivid and bodily, the bus itself, certain streets, and the experience of being alone with men became more charged over time, as though the memory had spread danger onto parts of his daily life.

What he made of these experiences hardened into a bleak view of other people and of himself. Minh had come to believe that you can never really know who will harm you, and that people cannot be trusted even when they appear gentle or concerned. When the memories hit with that much force, he took their vividness as proof that the threat had not truly ended. He also drew the conclusion that something about him was inadequate: if he had been stronger, more decisive, less naive, he thinks, he would have stopped it sooner or seen it coming. Those meanings did not sit in the background. They shaped what stood out to him, so that being alone with men, stepping onto a bus, or encountering anything that echoed the relationship pulled his attention immediately, already loaded with the expectation of harm.

That expectation now governs much of his day. If his girlfriend is late replying, if an editor takes longer than usual to text him back from an assignment, or if a source is delayed meeting him, Minh quickly assumes something bad is happening. At night he wakes and checks the apartment, listening for sounds and scanning for signs that he is not safe. Reassurance does little; even when someone tells him directly that he is safe, he cannot make himself believe it. Underneath that vigilance is the conviction that trust is dangerous and that he is not equipped to protect himself properly. The more he lives on alert, the more confirmed those beliefs feel to him.

His ways of coping have narrowed his life further. After being triggered on public transport or by a trauma-related scene while reporting, he goes over and over what he did wrong, replaying conversations and decisions with a punishing focus on his own failures. He never allows himself to feel or show anger about what was done to him; anger feels too risky, too close to losing control, so he turns it inward instead. On bad days he restricts food, describing it less as hunger loss than as something he does to get a grip on himself. These habits leave him feeling smaller, depleted, and more convinced of his own inadequacy. By trying not to feel anger, he ends up with more self-blame; by dwelling on his mistakes and undereating, he experiences himself as weak and damaged, which only deepens his mistrust and fear of harm.

His work has started to suffer in concrete ways. Journalism used to mean movement across the city, quick interviews, and long days following a story wherever it went. Now he avoids bus routes whenever he can, turns down some assignments that would leave him alone with male sources, and has become more hesitant in the field when meetings run late. His girlfriend has noticed that he startles awake and checks the locks, then lies rigid beside her, unconvinced by her attempts to calm him. Minh finally sought help after leaving an interview midway through, shaken by a male source stepping too close in a narrow hallway and then overwhelmed by pain and the sense that the abuse was happening again. What frightens him most is the feeling that danger has spread everywhere and that he can no longer trust his own judgment. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is to feel that the past is actually past and to move through his work and relationship without bracing for harm at every delay, every bus ride, every closed room.
